newsitem.title: USA: Pan Am to take to skies again next week.
newsitem.headline: Pan Am to take to skies again next week.

text.p: Pan Am, one of the great names of aviation until its collapse five years ago, will take to the skies again on Sept. 26, the company said Thursday.
The Department of Transportation gave its clearance Wednesday for the new Pan Am to begin operations.

The first flight will take off from Miami for New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport next Thursday, with another flight from New York to Los Angeles, spokesman Jeff Kriendler said. The airline will run one daily flight on each route.

Florida businessmen Chuck Cobb and Martin Shugrue bought the Pan Am name and logo in 1993 with the plan of eventually resurrecting the carrier, which had been one of the commerical aviation industry's pioneers. It collapsed in debt in 1991, weakened by the 1988 bombing over Lockerbie, Scotland, and stiff industry competition.
Shugrue previously served as vice chairman and chief operating officer of the old Pan Am.
The new Pan Am is a modest outfit in comparison with its namesake, offering cheap fares and hoping to reap the benefits of an illustrious name.
The old Pan Am, which flew from 1927 until it collapsed, is still being liquidated in a federal bankruptcy court. Cobb paid $1.3 million for the Pan Am name and logo from the estate.
The new airline will use the traditional blue and white colours and styles of its namesake.
"If you go to the airport, you'd think you were in a time warp. It's all the same," Kriendler said.
The airline began taking bookings Thursday, although its first advertisements will not appear until the weekend.
"The process has begun. We expect a lot of aviation buffs on that first flight," Kriendler said.
Many veterans of the old Pan Am are among the 400 employees, who include about 55 pilots.

The new Miami-based fleet totals two Airbus A-300 jets, with a third to be delivered next week. Expansion plans envisage having eight planes by the end of the first year, all on domestic routes, Kriendler said.
"The pricing will be very affordable and we're going to out-do our competitors with our service," he added.

The carrier said that contrary to industry practice, it will not impose Saturday night stay-over requirements or advance purchase restrictions. It also said it will not charge fees to change non-refundable tickets.
The airline said it will have a simplified fare structure, with all seats in each class of service available at the same price during the introductory period lasting until Nov. 24.

Government clearance for Pan Am was given despite objections by relatives of victims of the ill-fated Flight 103 which blew up over Lockerbie, Scotland, in December 1989, killing 270 people. The families opposed Shugrue's involvement with the carrier.
Kriendler conceded that by buying the Pan Am name and logo the company was also taking onboard a certain stigma from the bombing.
"Certainly there is the association," he said. "But most people have fond memories of Pan Am over the years and hopefully they will not be influenced by this tragedy."
